# How to use this guide

Pharmaceutical Microbiology rewards two things: **exact numbers** (121 °C, 15 psi, 15 min; 160 °C for 2 h; 0.22 µm; 25 kGy) and **clear, labelled diagrams** (bacterial cell, growth curve, autoclave, laminar flow cabinet, cup-plate assay). Read one unit a day, then redraw every diagram from memory before you open the question bank.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ or very short answers | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

Sessional (internal) marks of 25 are added separately in most colleges, and the practical BP307P is examined on its own with a separate paper, experiment, spotting and viva.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; learn the full answer with its diagram and numbers.
- **Medium** — asked every few years, or as one part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare in the written paper, but useful for Section A and for viva.

**Where the marks sit in this subject**

| Unit | Weight in the paper | Must-know topics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Heavy | Bacterial ultrastructure, growth curve, culture media, viable counts, microscopy |
| 2 | Heaviest | Gram and acid-fast staining, IMViC, moist and dry heat, radiation, filtration, ethylene oxide, sterility indicators |
| 3 | Moderate | Fungi and viruses, disinfectant classes, phenol coefficient, sterility testing |
| 4 | Moderate | Aseptic area design, laminar flow, clean area grades, cup-plate and turbidimetric assay |
| 5 | Moderate | Spoilage factors, preservatives, challenge test, types of cell culture |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. **Start with the definition.** Begin every answer with one clean sentence defining the term (sterilisation, disinfection, MIC, water activity). It is almost always worth a mark.
2. **Give the conditions.** Never write "autoclaving" alone — write 121 °C, 15 psi, 15 minutes. Marks follow numbers.
3. **Use a table for anything with two sides** — Gram-positive against Gram-negative, moist heat against dry heat, MIC against MBC, primary against continuous cell line. Tables are quicker to write and easier to mark.
4. **Draw before you write.** Label the bacterial cell, the growth curve with its four phases, the autoclave, the laminar flow cabinet and the cup-plate design. A labelled diagram earns marks even when the words run short.
5. **Name the organism.** Examiners look for *Geobacillus stearothermophilus* for autoclave indicators, *Bacillus atrophaeus* for dry heat and ethylene oxide, *Bacillus pumilus* for radiation, *Brevundimonas diminuta* for filters, *Salmonella typhi* for the phenol coefficient, *Lactobacillus leichmannii* for vitamin B12. Write species names in full the first time.
6. **End with uses.** Two or three pharmaceutical applications close an answer well, because this is an applied subject: which products are sterilised that way, which preservative goes into eye drops, which cell line makes a vaccine.
7. **Keep the words separate.** Sterilisation kills everything including spores; disinfection does not; antisepsis is on living tissue; preservation stops growth during use. Mixing them up loses easy marks.
8. **For mechanism questions, write the steps in order** — the stain steps, the stages of virus replication, the phases of the growth curve — and number them.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only one hour, learn these five with full diagrams: **moist heat and dry heat sterilisation with conditions**, **Gram staining with its mechanism**, **the bacterial growth curve**, **aseptic area and laminar flow**, and **the cup-plate microbiological assay**. Together they cover most of the 10-mark questions.

**Numbers to carry into the hall**

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Autoclave | 121 °C, 15 psi, 15 min (also 115 °C/30 min, 126 °C/10 min, 134 °C/3 min) |
| Hot air oven | 160 °C for 2 h (170 °C/1 h, 180 °C/30 min) |
| Depyrogenation of glass | about 250 °C or above |
| Pasteurisation | 63 °C for 30 min (holder); 72 °C for 15 s (flash) |
| Tyndallisation | 100 °C, 20–30 min, on 3 successive days |
| Sterilising filter | 0.22 µm; sterility test membrane 0.45 µm |
| Gamma radiation dose | 25 kGy (2.5 Mrad), cobalt-60 |
| Germicidal UV | 254 nm (DNA absorbs near 260 nm) |
| HEPA filter | retains at least 99.97% of 0.3 µm particles |
| Laminar flow velocity | about 0.45 m/s (90 ft/min) |
| Sterility test incubation | 14 days; thioglycollate 30–35 °C, soyabean–casein digest 20–25 °C |
| Sterility assurance level | 10⁻⁶ |
| Bacterial cell size | 0.5–5 µm; viruses 20–300 nm |
| Light microscope resolution | about 0.2 µm; electron microscope about 0.2–0.5 nm |
| Agar in solid media | 1.5–2%; melts near 100 °C, sets near 40 °C |
| *E. coli* generation time | about 20 min in good conditions |
| Plate count range | 30–300 colonies per plate |
| Cell culture conditions | 37 °C, 5% CO2, pH 7.2–7.4, 5–10% serum |

**Stains at a glance**

| Stain | Steps | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gram | Crystal violet → iodine → alcohol → safranin | Positive purple, negative pink |
| Ziehl–Neelsen | Hot carbol fuchsin → 20% H2SO4 → methylene blue | Acid-fast red on blue background |
| Endospore (Schaeffer–Fulton) | Malachite green with heat → safranin | Spore green, cell red |
| Capsule | India ink or nigrosin (negative stain) | Clear halo round the cell |

**IMViC**

| Organism | Indole | Methyl red | Voges–Proskauer | Citrate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *Escherichia coli* | + | + | − | − |
| *Enterobacter aerogenes* | − | − | + | + |

**Biological indicators**

| Process | Indicator organism |
| --- | --- |
| Moist heat | *Geobacillus stearothermophilus* |
| Dry heat and ethylene oxide | *Bacillus atrophaeus* |
| Ionising radiation | *Bacillus pumilus* |
| Filtration challenge | *Brevundimonas diminuta* |

**Mechanisms in one line each**

| Agent | How it kills |
| --- | --- |
| Moist heat | Coagulates and denatures proteins |
| Dry heat | Oxidises cell constituents |
| Ionising radiation | Free radicals break DNA |
| Ultraviolet | Thymine dimers block replication |
| Ethylene oxide | Alkylates proteins and nucleic acids |
| Phenols | Damage membrane, leakage; denature protein |
| Alcohol 70% | Denatures protein, dissolves lipids |
| Hypochlorite and iodine | Oxidation of cell proteins |
| Aldehydes | Alkylation |
| Quaternary ammonium compounds | Disrupt the cell membrane |
| Heavy metals | Bind sulphydryl groups of enzymes |

**Comparisons worth memorising**

| Pair | Key difference |
| --- | --- |
| Sterilisation / disinfection | Spores killed / spores may survive |
| Moist heat / dry heat | 121 °C, 15 min, coagulation / 160 °C, 2 h, oxidation |
| Gram-positive / Gram-negative | Thick peptidoglycan with teichoic acid / thin wall with outer membrane and endotoxin |
| Prokaryote / eukaryote | No nuclear membrane, 70S ribosomes / true nucleus, 80S ribosomes |
| Total count / viable count | Counts dead cells too / only living, as CFU |
| MIC / MBC | Stops visible growth / kills 99.9% |
| Cup-plate / turbidimetric assay | Zone diameter in 18–24 h / turbidity in 3–4 h |
| Primary / continuous cell line | From tissue, limited life / immortal, often aneuploid |

**Test organisms to name**

| Purpose | Organism |
| --- | --- |
| Phenol coefficient | *Salmonella typhi* |
| Vitamin B12 assay | *Lactobacillus leichmannii* |
| Riboflavin assay | *Lactobacillus casei* |
| Antibiotic assays | *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Bacillus subtilis*, *Bacillus pumilus*, *Micrococcus luteus* (per monograph) |
| Preservative challenge test | *S. aureus*, *P. aeruginosa*, *E. coli*, *C. albicans*, *A. brasiliensis* |

**Clean area grades:** A critical zone with unidirectional air (filling and open containers) → B background room → C and D supporting rooms. Positive pressure, air locks, HEPA filters, coved corners, people are the biggest source of contamination.

**Growth curve:** lag (adapting) → log (fastest, most sensitive, used in assays) → stationary (nutrients low, spores and antibiotics formed) → decline (death exceeds division).

**Virus replication:** adsorption → penetration → uncoating → biosynthesis (eclipse) → assembly → release.

**Spoilage checklist:** water activity, nutrients, pH, temperature, oxygen, packaging, formulation, contamination level, handling in use.

# Study of laboratory equipment and processes

**Aim:** To study the construction, working principle and uses of the equipment used in a microbiology laboratory: BOD incubator, laminar air flow unit, aseptic hood, autoclave, hot air oven, colony counter and compound microscope.

> Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where details differ. Wear a lab coat, tie back long hair and never work at an autoclave or oven that is still under pressure or hot.

## Principle

Microbiological work needs three things: a way to kill organisms on apparatus and media (autoclave, hot air oven), a clean space to work in without adding new organisms (laminar flow unit, aseptic hood), and a controlled place for wanted organisms to grow (incubator). Counting and observation equipment complete the set.

## Requirements

BOD incubator, laminar air flow unit, autoclave (vertical or horizontal), hot air oven, colony counter, compound microscope with oil immersion objective, refrigerator, hot plate, weighing balance.

## Procedure

1. **BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) incubator.** Note the double wall with insulation, the heating element, the cooling coil, the thermostat and the perforated shelves. It can both heat and cool, so it holds a set temperature between about 5 °C and 60 °C. Set it to 37 °C for bacteria and to 25 °C for fungi, and record how long it takes to steady.
2. **Laminar air flow unit.** Note the pre-filter, blower, HEPA filter, work surface and ultraviolet lamp. Switch on the ultraviolet lamp for 15–20 minutes with the sash closed, switch it off, run the blower for 15 minutes, swab the surface with 70% alcohol, and then work at least 15 cm inside the front edge. Record the air velocity shown on the gauge (about 0.45 m/s).
3. **Aseptic hood (inoculation chamber).** A small enclosed cabinet disinfected with alcohol or formaldehyde and fitted with an ultraviolet lamp; used for transfers where a full laminar flow unit is not available.
4. **Autoclave.** Identify the chamber, lid with gasket and clamps, water level mark, heating element, pressure gauge, safety valve, air-escape (steam) valve and drain. Load, expel the air, hold at 121 °C and 15 psi for 15 minutes, and allow the pressure to return to zero before opening.
5. **Hot air oven.** Identify the double wall, heating coils, thermostat, fan and perforated shelves. Sterilise dry glassware at 160 °C for 2 hours and cool inside the oven before removing.
6. **Colony counter.** Note the illuminated base, magnifying lens, grid plate and counting pen or digital counter. Place a plate on the grid and count colonies square by square.
7. **Compound microscope.** Identify the eyepiece, objectives (10x, 45x, 100x oil immersion), condenser with iris diaphragm, stage, coarse and fine adjustments and light source. Focus a prepared slide under low power first, then add a drop of immersion oil for the 100x objective.

## Observations

| Equipment | Working conditions set | Chief use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BOD incubator | 37 °C (bacteria), 25 °C (fungi) | Growing cultures |
| Laminar air flow | about 0.45 m/s through a HEPA filter | Contamination-free working space |
| Autoclave | 121 °C, 15 psi, 15 min | Media, aqueous liquids, discarded cultures |
| Hot air oven | 160 °C, 2 h | Dry glassware, powders, oils |
| Colony counter | — | Viable counts |
| Microscope | 100x with oil | Stained bacterial smears |

## Result

The construction, working and applications of the equipment listed above were studied and recorded.

## Precautions

1. Never open the autoclave until the pressure gauge reads zero.
2. Do not look at a lit ultraviolet lamp; switch it off before working.
3. Let glassware cool inside the hot air oven to prevent cracking.
4. Do not overload any sterilising equipment; air and steam must circulate.
5. Wipe the oil immersion lens with lens paper after use.

## Viva questions

1. **Why must air be removed from an autoclave?** An air–steam mixture is cooler than pure steam at the same pressure, and air pockets stop steam reaching the load.
2. **What does a HEPA filter retain?** At least 99.97% of particles of 0.3 µm diameter.
3. **Why is dry heat used at a higher temperature than moist heat?** Dry air carries less heat and penetrates poorly; it kills by oxidation, which is slower than coagulation of proteins by moist heat.
4. **What is the use of the iris diaphragm?** It controls the amount of light reaching the specimen, which adjusts contrast.
5. **Why is the BOD incubator preferred for fungi?** It can cool as well as heat, so it holds 25 °C even in a warm laboratory.

# Sterilisation of glassware and preparation of media

**Aim:** To clean and sterilise laboratory glassware and to sterilise prepared culture media, and to confirm that the sterilisation was effective.

> Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where details differ. Use heat-resistant gloves for hot glassware.

## Principle

Glassware is sterilised by **dry heat** in a hot air oven (160 °C for 2 hours), which kills organisms by oxidation. Culture media are aqueous and heat-stable, so they are sterilised by **moist heat** in an autoclave (121 °C, 15 psi, 15 minutes), which kills by coagulating proteins. Sugar-containing and gelatin media that cannot take 121 °C are sterilised by Tyndallisation at 100 °C on three successive days.

## Requirements

Test tubes, Petri dishes, pipettes, conical flasks, cotton, brown paper or aluminium foil, pipette cans, detergent, chromic acid or other cleaning solution, hot air oven, autoclave, prepared nutrient broth and agar, indicator tape or Browne's tubes.

## Procedure

**A. Cleaning and packing glassware**

1. Soak used glassware in disinfectant, then wash with detergent and a brush, rinse with tap water and finally with distilled water.
2. Dry the glassware completely; dry heat will not sterilise wet articles reliably.
3. Plug test tubes and flasks with non-absorbent cotton plugs, wrap Petri dishes in paper or foil, and place pipettes in metal cans with a plug of cotton at the mouthpiece end.
4. Attach a piece of indicator tape to a few packs.

**B. Dry heat sterilisation**

5. Arrange the packs on the oven shelves with space between them for air to move.
6. Heat at **160 °C for 2 hours**, counting the time only after the oven reaches 160 °C.
7. Switch off and let the oven cool before removing the glassware.

**C. Moist heat sterilisation of media**

8. Dispense the prepared broth or molten agar into tubes or flasks, plug them and cover the plugs with paper.
9. Fill the autoclave to the water mark, load the containers loosely and close the lid with the air valve open.
10. Allow steam to escape steadily to drive out the air, close the valve, and let the pressure rise to **15 psi (121 °C)**. Hold for **15 minutes**.
11. Switch off, allow the pressure to fall to zero on its own, then open the lid and remove the containers. Slope the agar tubes for slants, or cool them to about 45 °C before pouring plates.

**D. Checking the sterilisation**

12. Note the colour change of the indicator tape or the Browne's tube.
13. Incubate two uninoculated tubes of the sterilised medium at 37 °C for 24–48 hours. No growth means the medium is sterile.

## Observations

| Article | Method | Conditions | Indicator result | Sterility check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Petri dishes, pipettes, test tubes | Dry heat | 160 °C, 2 h | | |
| Nutrient broth, nutrient agar | Moist heat | 121 °C, 15 psi, 15 min | | |

## Result

The glassware was sterilised by dry heat at 160 °C for 2 hours and the media by autoclaving at 121 °C and 15 psi for 15 minutes; the uninoculated control tubes showed no growth, so the sterilisation was effective.

## Precautions

1. Glassware must be completely dry before dry heat sterilisation.
2. Do not pack the oven or the autoclave tightly.
3. Close caps only loosely in the autoclave, or the containers may burst.
4. Never open the autoclave while it is under pressure.
5. Keep sterilised articles wrapped until the moment of use.

## Viva questions

1. **Why are media autoclaved and not baked?** They are aqueous; steam heats them quickly and evenly at a temperature low enough not to spoil the nutrients, while dry heat would evaporate and char them.
2. **Why is cotton used as a plug?** It lets air and steam pass but filters out organisms as the tube cools and draws in air.
3. **Which media cannot be autoclaved at 121 °C?** Those with sugars, gelatin, serum or vitamins; they are Tyndallised, filtered or autoclaved at a lower temperature.
4. **What does indicator tape prove?** Only that the pack was exposed to the process; it does not prove the organisms were killed.
5. **At what temperature is molten agar poured into plates?** About 45 °C, cool enough not to kill the inoculum and warm enough to stay liquid.

# Preparation of culture media for bacteria

**Aim:** To prepare nutrient broth, nutrient agar slants and nutrient agar plates, sterilise them and check them for sterility.

> Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where details differ.

## Principle

A culture medium supplies water, a nitrogen and carbon source, minerals and growth factors at a suitable pH. **Nutrient broth** is a simple liquid basal medium; adding 1.5–2% **agar**, which melts near 100 °C and sets near 40 °C and is not digested by most bacteria, makes a solid medium that can be poured as plates or set as slants.

## Requirements

Peptone, beef extract, sodium chloride, agar, distilled water, 0.1 N sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid, pH paper or pH meter, conical flasks, test tubes, Petri dishes, balance, hot plate, autoclave, laminar air flow unit.

## Formula (for 1000 ml)

| Ingredient | Nutrient broth | Nutrient agar | Role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Peptone | 5 g | 5 g | Nitrogen, amino acids |
| Beef extract | 3 g | 3 g | Vitamins, minerals, amino acids |
| Sodium chloride | 5 g | 5 g | Osmotic balance |
| Agar | — | 15–20 g | Solidifying agent |
| Distilled water | to 1000 ml | to 1000 ml | Solvent |
| Final pH | 7.2–7.4 | 7.2–7.4 | Suits most bacteria |

## Procedure

1. Weigh the ingredients accurately and dissolve peptone, beef extract and sodium chloride in about 800 ml of distilled water with gentle warming and stirring.
2. Adjust the pH to **7.2–7.4** with 0.1 N sodium hydroxide or hydrochloric acid; check with pH paper or a meter.
3. Make up to 1000 ml with distilled water.
4. For agar media, add the agar and heat with constant stirring until it dissolves completely and the liquid is clear. Do not let it boil over.
5. Dispense: about 5–10 ml of broth per tube; about 5 ml of molten agar per tube for slants; the rest in flasks for pouring plates.
6. Plug the tubes and flasks with cotton and cover with paper.
7. Autoclave at **121 °C and 15 psi for 15 minutes**.
8. **Slants:** lay the hot agar tubes on the bench at a slope so the agar sets with a long surface, leaving a short butt.
9. **Plates:** cool the flask to about 45 °C, and in the laminar air flow unit pour 15–20 ml into each sterile Petri dish; replace the lid at once and let it set on a level surface.
10. Incubate two tubes of each medium and two poured plates at 37 °C for 24 hours as a sterility check.

## Observations

| Medium | Appearance before sterilisation | Appearance after sterilisation | Sterility check (growth / no growth) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nutrient broth | Clear light amber liquid | | |
| Nutrient agar slant | Molten amber liquid | Firm sloped surface | |
| Nutrient agar plate | Molten amber liquid | Firm, smooth, no bubbles | |

## Result

Nutrient broth, nutrient agar slants and nutrient agar plates were prepared at pH 7.2–7.4, sterilised at 121 °C and 15 psi for 15 minutes, and found sterile after incubation at 37 °C for 24 hours.

## Precautions

1. Dissolve the agar completely before autoclaving, or the medium will set unevenly.
2. Adjust the pH before adding the agar and before sterilising.
3. Cool the agar to about 45 °C before pouring; hotter agar produces condensation, cooler agar sets in the flask.
4. Pour plates inside the laminar air flow unit and open the lid only slightly.
5. Let the plates set undisturbed on a level surface and store them inverted to stop condensation dropping onto the agar.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is agar preferred to gelatin?** It melts near 100 °C and sets near 40 °C, stays solid at 37 °C and is not digested by most bacteria, while gelatin melts at body temperature and is liquefied by many organisms.
2. **What is the purpose of peptone?** It supplies nitrogen as amino acids and peptides.
3. **Why is the pH set at 7.2–7.4?** Most medically important bacteria grow best near neutral pH.
4. **Why are plates stored inverted?** So that condensed water on the lid does not fall onto the agar surface and spread colonies.
5. **What would you add to make the medium selective for fungi?** Lower the pH to about 5.6 and use a high-glucose peptone medium, or add an antibacterial such as chloramphenicol.

# Sub-culturing of bacteria and fungi: stabs and slants

**Aim:** To transfer a given bacterial culture aseptically to fresh nutrient broth, a nutrient agar slant, a nutrient agar stab and a plate, to subculture a fungus on Sabouraud dextrose agar, and to observe the growth.

> Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where details differ. Treat every culture as infectious; disinfect the bench before and after work.

## Principle

Bacteria die when nutrients run out and waste collects, so stock cultures are kept alive by **sub-culturing**: transferring a small inoculum to fresh medium at intervals with a sterile loop or needle, using **aseptic technique** so that no other organism gets in and nothing escapes into the room.

## Requirements

Stock culture of a named organism (for example *Escherichia coli* or *Bacillus subtilis*), sterile nutrient broth tubes, nutrient agar slants, nutrient agar plates, nichrome inoculating loop and straight wire, Bunsen burner or spirit lamp, laminar air flow unit, incubator, marker pen, discard jar with disinfectant.

## Procedure

1. Disinfect the work surface with 70% alcohol and light the burner (or work in the laminar air flow unit).
2. Label each fresh tube or plate with the organism, your name, the date and the medium.
3. **Flame the loop** until it is red hot along its whole length, then let it cool for a few seconds near the flame without touching anything.
4. Hold the stock culture tube in the left hand. Remove the plug with the little finger of the right hand (the hand holding the loop), **flame the mouth** of the tube, and take a loopful of growth.
5. Flame the mouth again, replace the plug, and pick up the fresh tube.
6. **Broth:** remove the plug, flame the mouth, dip the loop in the broth and shake gently to release the inoculum, flame the mouth and replace the plug.
7. **Slant:** remove the plug, flame the mouth, and draw a single straight or zigzag line up the slope of the agar from the butt to the top without digging into the agar. Flame and replug.
8. **Plate:** lift the lid only enough to admit the loop and streak the surface lightly in a zigzag over one quadrant and then spread out.
9. **Flame the loop** again before putting it down, so nothing live is left on it.
10. **Stab culture.** Charge a sterile **straight wire** with growth and push it vertically into the centre of a tube of nutrient agar butt, almost to the bottom, withdrawing it along the same track. Stabs are used for motility, for anaerobic growth and for stock cultures.
11. **Fungal subculture.** Transfer a small piece of the mould or a loopful of yeast onto a **Sabouraud dextrose agar** slant with a straight wire, and incubate at 25 °C for 3–7 days; fungi grow slowly and prefer the lower temperature and the acidic medium.
12. Incubate at 37 °C for 24 hours: tubes upright, plates inverted.
13. Keep one uninoculated tube and one uninoculated plate as sterility controls.

## Observations

| Medium | Expected appearance of growth | Observed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nutrient broth | Uniform turbidity, or a surface pellicle or a sediment depending on the organism | |
| Nutrient agar slant | A continuous line of growth along the streak, with its own colour and texture | |
| Nutrient agar plate | Discrete or confluent colonies, described by size, shape, margin, elevation, colour and opacity | |
| Nutrient agar stab | Growth along the stab line, spreading outwards if the organism is motile | |
| Sabouraud slant (fungus) | Cottony, powdery or creamy growth after 3–7 days at 25 °C | |
| Uninoculated control | No growth | |

## Result

The given culture was sub-cultured aseptically into broth, onto a slant and onto a plate; growth appeared on all three after incubation at 37 °C for 24 hours, while the uninoculated controls remained clear, showing that the technique was aseptic.

## Precautions

1. Cool the flamed loop before touching the culture, or the heat will kill the cells and spatter them.
2. Never put the plug down on the bench; hold it in the hand.
3. Flame the mouth of every tube when opening and closing it.
4. Do not dig into the agar; the loop should glide over the surface.
5. Flame the loop before and after every transfer, and discard everything into disinfectant.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is the mouth of the tube flamed?** The hot air rising from the mouth stops airborne organisms from settling inside.
2. **Why is the loop made of nichrome or platinum?** These metals heat and cool quickly and do not corrode.
3. **What is the difference between a loop and a straight wire?** A loop carries a measured drop for surface streaking; a straight wire is used for stab cultures and for picking single colonies.
4. **Why are plates incubated upside down?** So that condensation on the lid does not drip onto the growth.
5. **Why are fungi subcultured at 25 °C on Sabouraud agar?** Most fungi grow best at 25–30 °C, and the high sugar content with an acidic pH of about 5.6 favours them while holding back bacteria.
6. **How often should a stock culture be sub-cultured?** Usually every few weeks when stored at 4 °C; long-term storage uses paraffin overlay, freezing or freeze-drying.

# Simple staining of bacteria

**Aim:** To prepare a bacterial smear and stain it with a single basic dye to study the shape, size and arrangement of the cells.

> Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where details differ. Stains mark skin and clothes; handle them over the sink on a staining rack.

## Principle

The bacterial cell surface carries a **negative charge**, so it attracts the coloured positive ion of a **basic dye** such as methylene blue, crystal violet or carbol fuchsin. One dye is used, so every cell takes the same colour; the stain therefore shows only **morphology** — shape, size and arrangement — and not any difference between organisms.

## Requirements

Young (18–24 hour) broth or slant culture, clean grease-free slides, inoculating loop, burner, staining rack, methylene blue (or crystal violet or carbol fuchsin), wash bottle of distilled water, blotting paper, immersion oil, microscope.

## Procedure

1. **Clean the slide** with alcohol and wipe dry; grease stops the smear from spreading.
2. **Make the smear.** For a slant culture, place a small drop of saline or water on the slide, add a little growth with a sterile loop and spread it into a thin film about the size of a coin. For a broth culture, spread one or two loopfuls directly.
3. **Air dry** the smear completely at room temperature; do not heat it while wet.
4. **Heat fix** by passing the slide, smear upwards, through the flame two or three times. The slide should feel warm, not hot. This kills the cells, makes them stick to the glass and helps them take the stain.
5. **Stain:** flood the smear with methylene blue for about 1 minute (crystal violet needs about 30–60 seconds, carbol fuchsin about 30 seconds).
6. **Wash** gently with a thin stream of water until no more colour runs off.
7. **Blot dry** between blotting paper; do not rub.
8. Examine under low power, then under the **oil immersion objective (100x)** with a drop of immersion oil.

## Observations

| Feature | What to look for | Observed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shape | Cocci (round), bacilli (rods), vibrio (comma), spirilla (spiral) | |
| Arrangement | Single, pairs, chains, clusters, tetrads | |
| Size | Compared with the field, roughly 0.5–5 µm | |
| Colour | Uniform colour of the dye used | |

Typical results: *Staphylococcus aureus* appears as blue cocci in grape-like clusters; *Escherichia coli* as blue short rods, single or in pairs; *Bacillus subtilis* as long rods, sometimes in chains.

## Result

The given culture was stained by the simple staining method and the cells were found to be ______ in shape and arranged in ______.

## Precautions

1. Make the smear thin; a thick smear makes the cells pile up and look distorted.
2. Dry the smear fully before fixing, or the cells will burst.
3. Do not over-heat during fixing; excess heat distorts the cells.
4. Wash gently, directing the water above the smear, so the film is not washed away.
5. Use a young culture; old cells stain unevenly and may look misshapen.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is a basic dye used?** The bacterial surface is negatively charged and binds the positively charged coloured part of a basic dye.
2. **What is the purpose of heat fixing?** It kills the organisms, sticks them to the slide and improves staining.
3. **What does a simple stain not tell you?** It cannot distinguish one organism from another, since every cell takes the same colour; it shows only shape and arrangement.
4. **What is negative staining?** An acidic dye such as nigrosin or India ink stains the background instead of the cell, so the unstained cell and its capsule stand out.
5. **Why is immersion oil used?** It has nearly the same refractive index as glass, so less light is lost by refraction and the resolving power of the 100x objective is realised.
practicals.title: Simple staining of bacteria

# Gram staining

**Aim:** To stain a given bacterial culture by Gram's method and to classify it as Gram-positive or Gram-negative.

> Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where details differ. The decolourising step decides the result, so time it carefully.

## Principle

Crystal violet enters every cell and is fixed by iodine as a large **crystal violet–iodine complex**. Alcohol then dehydrates the thick peptidoglycan of a **Gram-positive** wall, closing its pores so the complex is trapped, and the cell stays purple. In a **Gram-negative** cell alcohol dissolves the lipid-rich outer membrane and the thin peptidoglycan cannot hold the complex, so the cell loses the colour and is then stained pink by safranin.

## Requirements

18–24 hour cultures (for example *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Escherichia coli*), clean slides, loop, burner, staining rack, crystal violet solution, Gram's iodine, 95% ethanol (or acetone–alcohol), safranin, wash bottle, blotting paper, immersion oil, microscope.

## Procedure

1. Prepare a thin smear, air dry it and heat fix it as for simple staining.
2. Flood with **crystal violet** and leave for **1 minute**. Wash briefly with water.
3. Flood with **Gram's iodine** (the mordant) and leave for **1 minute**. Wash briefly.
4. **Decolourise** by letting 95% ethanol run down the tilted slide, drop by drop, for only a few seconds, until no more violet colour comes away. Wash at once with water to stop the action.
5. Counterstain with **safranin** for 30–60 seconds. Wash with water.
6. Blot dry and examine under the oil immersion objective.

```text
  Crystal violet  →  Iodine  →  Alcohol  →  Safranin
      purple          purple     Gram +ve stays purple     purple
      purple          purple     Gram −ve goes colourless  pink
```

## Observations

| Culture | Colour seen | Shape and arrangement | Gram reaction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Culture A | | | |
| Culture B | | | |

Typical results: *Staphylococcus aureus* — purple cocci in clusters, Gram-positive. *Escherichia coli* — pink short rods, Gram-negative.

## Result

The given culture stained ______ and was found to be **Gram-______** with ______ shaped cells.

## Precautions

1. Use a young culture. Old Gram-positive cells lose the ability to hold the dye and may appear Gram-negative.
2. The smear must be thin; thick areas decolourise unevenly.
3. Do not over-decolourise. This is the commonest cause of a false Gram-negative result; stop as soon as the running alcohol is clear.
4. Wash immediately after the alcohol step.
5. Always run a known Gram-positive and a known Gram-negative control alongside an unknown.

## Viva questions

1. **Who developed this stain and when?** Christian Gram, in 1884.
2. **What is the role of iodine here?** It acts as a mordant, forming a large complex with crystal violet inside the cell so the dye is not easily washed out.
3. **Which step is critical and why?** Decolourising with alcohol, because the difference between the two groups depends entirely on how much colour is removed.
4. **Why does a Gram-positive cell retain the colour?** Its thick multilayered peptidoglycan with teichoic acid dehydrates and traps the complex; the Gram-negative wall is thin and its outer lipid membrane is dissolved away.
5. **Name two organisms of each type.** Gram-positive: *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Bacillus subtilis*. Gram-negative: *Escherichia coli*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*.
6. **Why does the Gram reaction matter clinically?** It guides the first choice of antibiotic before the full report is available.
practicals.title: Gram staining

# Acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen) staining

**Aim:** To stain a given smear by the Ziehl-Neelsen method and to detect acid-fast bacilli.

> Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where details differ. In teaching laboratories a safe demonstration organism or a prepared slide is used, not a pathogen; handle the acid solution with care and never heat the stain to boiling.

## Principle

The wall of *Mycobacterium* contains a large amount of waxy **mycolic acid**, so ordinary dyes do not enter. Heating with phenol-containing **carbol fuchsin** softens the wax and drives the dye in. Once inside, the dye is held so firmly that even a strong acid cannot remove it — the cell is **acid-fast** and stays red. All other cells lose the red dye in acid and take the blue counterstain.

## Requirements

Smear (sputum smear for demonstration or a prepared slide), strong carbol fuchsin, 20% sulphuric acid (or 3% acid-alcohol), methylene blue, staining rack, burner or spirit lamp with a swab on a holder, forceps, wash bottle, blotting paper, immersion oil, microscope.

## Procedure

1. Prepare a thin smear, air dry it and heat fix it.
2. Flood the slide with **strong carbol fuchsin**.
3. **Heat the underside of the slide gently** with a flame until steam just rises. Keep it steaming for about **5 minutes**, adding more stain so the smear never dries. Do not boil.
4. Let the slide cool, then wash with water.
5. **Decolourise** with **20% sulphuric acid** for 2–3 minutes, or until the smear is pale pink. Wash with water. Repeat if colour still comes away.
6. Counterstain with **methylene blue** for about 1 minute. Wash with water.
7. Blot dry and examine under the oil immersion objective, scanning several fields.

## Observations

| Structure | Colour | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acid-fast bacilli | Bright red or pink slender rods, often slightly curved, singly or in small groups | Acid-fast organism present |
| Other cells, pus cells, background | Blue | Non-acid-fast |

## Result

The given smear showed ______ acid-fast bacilli, so the organism is (acid-fast / non-acid-fast).

## Precautions

1. Keep the stain steaming but never boiling, and never let the slide dry during heating.
2. Add more carbol fuchsin during heating as it evaporates.
3. Cool the slide before washing so the glass does not crack.
4. Decolourise fully; the background must be free of red, or blue cells may be mistaken for acid-fast bacilli.
5. Use a fresh slide for each smear and dispose of slides in disinfectant.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is the stain heated?** Heat and phenol help the dye pass through the waxy mycolic acid layer of the wall.
2. **What does "acid-fast" mean?** The cell holds the primary stain even when treated with a strong acid, so it does not decolourise.
3. **Which component of the wall is responsible?** Mycolic acid, with other long-chain lipids.
4. **Why is a weaker acid used for *Mycobacterium leprae*?** It is less strongly acid-fast, so 5% sulphuric acid is used to avoid losing the stain.
5. **Name a modification that avoids heating.** The cold method using a stain with a wetting agent, and fluorescent staining with auramine, which is examined under a fluorescence microscope.
practicals.title: Acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen) staining

# Motility by the hanging drop method

**Aim:** To find out whether a given bacterial culture is motile, using a hanging drop preparation.

> Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where details differ. The preparation contains live organisms; seal and discard it in disinfectant.

## Principle

Motile bacteria swim by means of flagella. In a **hanging drop** a drop of young broth culture hangs from a coverslip over the hollow of a cavity slide, so the organisms are seen alive and unstained in a thin layer of fluid. True motility is a **directional, purposeful movement** of individual cells from one field to another; it must be told apart from **Brownian movement**, which is a trembling in one place caused by the bombardment of water molecules, and from **drift**, in which all the cells move together in one direction with the current.

## Requirements

Young (6–18 hour) broth culture of a motile organism (for example *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, *Proteus* or *Bacillus subtilis*) and of a non-motile organism (*Staphylococcus aureus* or *Klebsiella*), cavity (depression) slide, coverslip, petroleum jelly or wax, inoculating loop, burner, microscope.

## Procedure

1. Clean the cavity slide and the coverslip and dry them.
2. Place a small ring of petroleum jelly round the edge of the coverslip, using a matchstick.
3. Place **one loopful** of the young broth culture in the centre of the coverslip. Keep the drop small, or it will touch the slide.
4. Invert the cavity slide over the coverslip so that the hollow lies exactly over the drop and the jelly touches the slide.
5. Press gently and turn the slide the right way up quickly. The drop now hangs from the coverslip inside the sealed cavity.
6. Examine first under low power with the **iris diaphragm nearly closed** to get contrast, focusing on the edge of the drop.
7. Switch to the high-power (45x) objective and watch several fields for 2–3 minutes.

```text
   coverslip  ____________________
              |      · drop ·     |   <- culture hangs down
              |  ___/        \___ |
   slide  ____|_/   cavity     \_ |____
              petroleum jelly seal
```

## Observations

| Culture | Movement seen | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Organism A | Cells darting across the field, changing direction | Motile |
| Organism B | Cells trembling in one place only | Non-motile (Brownian movement) |

## Result

The given organism (is / is not) motile by the hanging drop method.

## Precautions

1. Use a young actively growing broth culture; motility is lost in old cultures.
2. Keep the drop small so it hangs free and does not spread.
3. Seal the cavity with jelly, or the drop dries and currents form.
4. Reduce the light with the iris diaphragm; a bright field makes unstained cells invisible.
5. Do not mistake drift (all cells moving the same way) or Brownian movement (trembling in place) for true motility.

## Viva questions

1. **What is Brownian movement?** A trembling of particles caused by collisions with water molecules; the cells do not change position.
2. **Name two motile and two non-motile bacteria.** Motile: *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, *Proteus vulgaris*. Non-motile: *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, *Staphylococcus aureus*.
3. **What other method shows motility?** Stabbing a semi-solid motility medium: motile organisms grow out from the stab line and turn the medium turbid; a motility indicator medium with tetrazolium shows the spread as colour.
4. **Why is the light reduced?** Unstained living cells have little contrast, which is improved by closing the iris diaphragm.
5. **What structure gives motility?** The flagellum, a protein filament of flagellin anchored in the cell envelope.
practicals.title: Motility by the hanging drop method

practicals.markdown:
# Isolation of a pure culture by streak plate

**Aim:** To isolate a pure culture from a mixed culture by the quadrant streak plate method and to describe the colonies obtained.

> Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where details differ.

## Principle

A **pure culture** contains only one kind of organism. In the **streak plate** method a loopful of a mixed culture is dragged over the agar in a series of linked strokes, each starting from the previous one. Cells are left behind at every stroke, so by the last sector single cells are separated far enough apart that each grows into a separate **colony** — a visible mass of cells descended from one cell. Picking one well-separated colony and transferring it to fresh medium gives a pure culture.

## Requirements

Mixed broth culture, sterile nutrient agar plates, inoculating loop, burner or laminar air flow unit, incubator, marker pen, colony counter or hand lens, discard jar.

## Procedure

1. Label the base of the plate with the organism, date and your name, and mark it into four sectors.
2. Flame the loop, cool it, and take one loopful of the mixed culture.
3. **Sector 1:** lift the lid slightly and streak the loopful back and forth close together over about a quarter of the plate.
4. **Flame the loop and cool it.** Turn the plate about 90°, and draw the loop three or four times through the end of sector 1, then streak out into sector 2 without re-entering sector 1 afterwards.
5. **Flame and cool the loop again.** Repeat from the end of sector 2 into sector 3, and once more into sector 4, so the inoculum becomes thinner at each step.
6. Flame the loop before putting it down.
7. Invert the plate and incubate at 37 °C for 24–48 hours.
8. Examine the plate: the first sector shows confluent growth, the last sector well-separated colonies.
9. Pick a single, well-separated colony with a sterile loop and sub-culture it onto a slant. This is the pure culture; confirm it by a Gram-stained smear showing one type of cell.

```text
        /  2  \         Each sector starts from the previous one,
       | ----- |        with the loop flamed in between, so the
       | 1   3 |        number of cells carried over falls sharply.
        \  4  /         Sector 4 should give single colonies.
```

## Observations

Describe the colonies in the last sector:

| Character | Possible descriptions | Observed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Size | Pinpoint, small, moderate, large | |
| Shape (form) | Circular, irregular, filamentous | |
| Margin | Entire, undulate, lobate, filamentous | |
| Elevation | Flat, raised, convex, umbonate | |
| Surface | Smooth, rough, wrinkled | |
| Colour (pigment) | White, cream, yellow, green | |
| Opacity | Transparent, translucent, opaque | |
| Haemolysis (on blood agar) | None, partial (alpha), complete (beta) | |

## Result

A pure culture was isolated from the mixed culture by the quadrant streak plate method; the colonies obtained were ______ and a Gram-stained smear showed a single type of cell.

## Precautions

1. Cool the loop after flaming, or the heat will kill the inoculum and spatter the culture.
2. Do not dig into or tear the agar.
3. Open the lid only as much as needed and for as short a time as possible.
4. Do not return to an earlier sector after flaming, or the dilution effect is lost.
5. Invert the plates for incubation.

## Viva questions

1. **Define a colony.** A visible group of cells on solid medium that has grown from a single cell or a single clump, so it is one colony-forming unit.
2. **Name other methods of obtaining a pure culture.** Pour plate, spread plate, serial dilution in broth, use of selective and enrichment media, and single-cell picking with a micromanipulator.
3. **Why is the loop flamed between sectors?** To reduce the number of cells carried into the next sector, which is what separates the colonies.
4. **In the pour plate method, why is the agar cooled to about 45 °C?** Hotter agar would kill the organisms; cooler agar would set before mixing.
5. **How would you confirm a culture is pure?** All colonies look alike, a Gram-stained smear shows one type of cell, and biochemical tests give one consistent pattern.
practicals.title: Isolation of a pure culture by streak plate

# Biochemical identification by IMViC tests

**Aim:** To perform the indole, methyl red, Voges-Proskauer and citrate tests on given cultures and to distinguish *Escherichia coli* from *Enterobacter aerogenes*.

> Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where details differ. Kovac's and Barritt's reagents are corrosive; add them carefully.

## Principle

Different enteric bacteria break down the same nutrients by different routes, and the products can be detected with simple reagents.

- **Indole:** the enzyme tryptophanase splits tryptophan into indole, pyruvate and ammonia. Indole reacts with the aldehyde in Kovac's reagent to give a red compound that collects in the alcohol layer on top.
- **Methyl red:** organisms using the mixed-acid pathway produce so much acid that the pH falls to about 4.4 or lower, where methyl red is red.
- **Voges-Proskauer:** organisms using the butanediol pathway form acetoin, which is oxidised in air and alkali to diacetyl; this reacts with a component of peptone in the presence of alpha-naphthol to give a pink colour.
- **Citrate:** an organism able to use citrate as its only carbon source grows on the medium and releases alkaline products, turning the bromothymol blue indicator from green to blue.

## Requirements

24-hour cultures of *E. coli* and *Enterobacter aerogenes*, tryptone (peptone) water, glucose phosphate (MR-VP) broth, Simmons citrate agar slants, Kovac's reagent, methyl red solution, Barritt's reagents (5% alpha-naphthol in alcohol and 40% potassium hydroxide), sterile loop and straight wire, burner, incubator at 37 °C.

## Procedure

**Indole test**

1. Inoculate tryptone water with the test organism and incubate at 37 °C for 24–48 hours.
2. Add about 0.5 ml of Kovac's reagent down the side of the tube and shake gently. Read within a minute.

**Methyl red test**

3. Inoculate MR-VP broth and incubate at 37 °C for 48 hours (a shorter time can give a false negative).
4. Add 5 drops of methyl red solution to about 5 ml of the culture and read at once.

**Voges-Proskauer test**

5. Inoculate a second tube of MR-VP broth and incubate for 48 hours.
6. Add 0.6 ml of alpha-naphthol solution and then 0.2 ml of 40% potassium hydroxide, shake well and leave the tube slanted for 15–30 minutes, shaking occasionally to let air in.

**Citrate test**

7. Streak the surface of a Simmons citrate slant with a straight wire carrying a light inoculum (do not carry over nutrients from the previous medium).
8. Incubate at 37 °C for 24–48 hours with the cap loose, since the test needs air.

**Controls:** include an uninoculated tube of each medium.

## Observations

| Test | Positive result | Negative result | *E. coli* | *E. aerogenes* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Indole | Red ring in the alcohol layer | Yellow layer | | |
| Methyl red | Red | Yellow | | |
| Voges-Proskauer | Pink to red in 15–30 min | No colour change | | |
| Citrate | Blue, with growth on the slant | Green, no growth | | |

Expected pattern: *Escherichia coli* + + − − and *Enterobacter aerogenes* − − + +.

## Result

The given organism gave the pattern ______ and is therefore identified as ______.

## Precautions

1. Use a pure, fresh culture and label every tube.
2. Incubate the MR and VP tubes for a full 48 hours before adding reagents.
3. Add alpha-naphthol before potassium hydroxide in the Voges-Proskauer test, and shake to admit air.
4. Use a very light inoculum for citrate and keep the cap loose; carried-over nutrients give a false positive.
5. Read the indole test soon after adding Kovac's reagent, as the colour fades.

## Viva questions

1. **What does IMViC stand for?** Indole, Methyl red, Voges-Proskauer, Citrate; the small "i" is only for pronunciation.
2. **Why are two separate tubes used for MR and VP?** The tests are read at different times and each needs its own reagents; they are both performed on the same medium but cannot be done on one tube.
3. **What is the active ingredient of Kovac's reagent?** p-Dimethylaminobenzaldehyde in amyl alcohol with hydrochloric acid.
4. **Why does the citrate test need an alkaline shift?** Using citrate as the sole carbon source releases ammonia and carbonates, raising the pH so bromothymol blue turns blue.
5. **What is the importance of IMViC in pharmacy?** It helps identify coliforms in water and in microbial limit testing, where *E. coli* is an objectionable organism in oral products.

# Microbiological assay of an antibiotic by the cup-plate method

**Aim:** To determine the potency of a given antibiotic sample by the cup-plate (agar diffusion) method, comparing it with a standard preparation.

> Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where details differ.

## Principle

An antibiotic placed in a cup cut in seeded agar diffuses outwards, and its concentration falls as it spreads. Growth of the test organism is prevented up to the distance where the concentration is still above the inhibitory level, giving a clear **zone of inhibition**. Within a working range, the **diameter of the zone is proportional to the logarithm of the concentration**. By measuring zones for known concentrations of a **standard** and for the **test** solution under identical conditions, the potency of the test sample is calculated.

## Requirements

Standard antibiotic solution of known potency, test antibiotic sample, sterile nutrient agar (base and seed layers), culture of the specified test organism (for example *Staphylococcus aureus* or *Bacillus subtilis* as directed by the monograph), sterile Petri dishes, sterile cork borer (6–8 mm), sterile pipettes, phosphate buffer of the stated pH, laminar air flow unit, incubator, zone reader or vernier calliper.

## Procedure

1. Prepare the dilutions. From the standard, prepare two doses, for example S1 (low) and S2 (high), differing by a fixed ratio such as 1:2. Prepare the test sample at the same two expected levels, T1 and T2, in the same buffer.
2. Pour about 15 ml of molten nutrient agar into each Petri dish as a **base layer** and let it set on a level surface.
3. Cool a second portion of agar to about 45 °C, add the standardised inoculum of the test organism, mix without forming bubbles, and pour it over the base as a thin **seed layer**. Let it set.
4. With a sterile borer, cut four cups in each plate at equal distances from the centre and from each other, and remove the agar plugs with a sterile needle.
5. Fill the cups with equal volumes (for example 0.1 ml) of S1, S2, T1 and T2 in a **balanced arrangement**, so that each solution occupies each position equally often across the set of plates.
6. Keep the plates at room temperature (or 4 °C) for about an hour so the solutions diffuse before growth begins.
7. Incubate at 37 °C for 18–24 hours.
8. Measure the diameter of each zone of inhibition with a zone reader or calliper, taking two readings at right angles and averaging them.

```text
      ┌─────────────────────────────┐
      │        (S1)       (T1)      │   cups 6–8 mm, equally spaced
      │     ( clear zones round     │   S = standard, T = test
      │       each cup )            │   positions rotated between plates
      │        (T2)       (S2)      │
      └─────────────────────────────┘
```

## Observations and calculation

| Solution | Concentration | Zone diameter (mm), plate 1 | Plate 2 | Plate 3 | Mean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S1 (standard, low) | | | | | |
| S2 (standard, high) | | | | | |
| T1 (test, low) | | | | | |
| T2 (test, high) | | | | | |

**By standard curve:** plot mean zone diameter against log concentration for the standard; the points fall on a straight line. Read the log concentration of the test from its mean zone diameter and take the antilog.

**By the two-dose formula:**

log of potency ratio = ( (T1 + T2) − (S1 + S2) ) ÷ ( (S2 + T2) − (S1 + T1) ) × log of the dose ratio

Potency of the sample = antilog of the above × potency of the standard.

*Worked example:* S1 = 16.0 mm, S2 = 20.0 mm, T1 = 16.8 mm, T2 = 20.8 mm, dose ratio 2 (log 2 = 0.301).

- (T1 + T2) − (S1 + S2) = 37.6 − 36.0 = 1.6
- (S2 + T2) − (S1 + T1) = 40.8 − 32.8 = 8.0
- log ratio = (1.6 ÷ 8.0) × 0.301 = 0.0602; antilog = 1.15

The sample is about 1.15 times as potent as the assumed value, so if it was assumed to be 1000 units per ml, the found potency is about 1150 units per ml.

## Result

The potency of the given antibiotic sample was found to be ______ units (or µg) per ml, that is ______ per cent of the labelled potency.

## Precautions

1. Keep the layer of seeded agar of the same thickness in every plate; thickness changes the zone size.
2. Use a standardised inoculum; a heavier inoculum gives smaller zones.
3. Cool the agar to about 45 °C before adding the inoculum.
4. Fill all cups to the same level, without spilling on the surface.
5. Allow a diffusion period before incubation, and keep temperature and time identical for all plates.
6. Use the balanced (rotated) arrangement of solutions to cancel out plate-to-plate differences.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is zone diameter related to the logarithm of concentration?** Diffusion from the cup gives a concentration gradient that falls steeply with distance, so a geometric increase in dose produces an arithmetic increase in zone diameter.
2. **Why is a standard preparation needed?** Biological activity is compared, not measured absolutely; the standard defines the unit of potency.
3. **What is the advantage of a microbiological assay over a chemical assay?** It measures the actual antimicrobial activity, including that of mixtures and of substances with no convenient chemical method.
4. **Name the alternative method and its advantage.** The turbidimetric method, which gives a result in 3–4 hours instead of 18–24 hours.
5. **What happens if the plates are not level?** The agar layer varies in thickness, so zone diameters vary and the assay is invalid.
practicals.title: Microbiological assay of an antibiotic by the cup-plate method

# Sterility testing of a pharmaceutical product

**Aim:** To test a given parenteral or ophthalmic product for sterility by the membrane filtration and direct inoculation methods.

> Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where details differ. The test must be carried out under strict aseptic conditions, or a false positive result will follow.

## Principle

A sterility test shows whether viable organisms can be recovered from a product when it is incubated in media that support a wide range of organisms. **Fluid thioglycollate medium** (incubated at 30–35 °C) supports anaerobes and aerobes; **soyabean-casein digest medium** (incubated at 20–25 °C) supports aerobes, yeasts and moulds. Incubation runs for **not less than 14 days**. Because only a sample is tested, a pass supports but does not prove the sterility of the whole batch; it is one part of a validated process.

## Requirements

Test product (ampoules, vials or eye drops), fluid thioglycollate medium, soyabean-casein digest medium, sterile membrane filtration assembly with **0.45 µm** membranes, sterile rinsing fluid, sterile syringes and needles, forceps, 70% alcohol swabs, laminar air flow unit or isolator, incubators at 30–35 °C and 20–25 °C.

## Procedure

**A. Preparation**

1. Confirm by the growth promotion test that each batch of medium supports growth of the specified organisms, and that the media were sterile on incubation.
2. Disinfect the laminar air flow unit and all surfaces; wear sterile gloves and gown.
3. Disinfect the neck of each ampoule or the closure of each vial with 70% alcohol and let it dry.

**B. Membrane filtration method (preferred)**

4. Assemble the sterile filtration unit with a 0.45 µm membrane and wet it with sterile rinsing fluid.
5. Withdraw the contents of the required number of containers aseptically and transfer them to the funnel; apply suction so the liquid passes through, leaving any organisms on the membrane.
6. Rinse the membrane with sterile rinsing fluid (usually three rinses) to wash out any antibiotic or preservative that would stop growth.
7. Cut the membrane aseptically into two halves (or use two units): place one half in fluid thioglycollate medium and the other in soyabean-casein digest medium.

**C. Direct inoculation method**

8. For small volumes or products that cannot be filtered, transfer a measured volume of the product directly into each medium, keeping the volume of product small compared with the medium so that any antimicrobial substance is diluted out.

**D. Controls and incubation**

9. Keep uninoculated containers of each medium as **negative controls**.
10. Incubate thioglycollate tubes at **30–35 °C** and soyabean-casein digest tubes at **20–25 °C** for **14 days**.
11. Examine on alternate days and on the fourteenth day for turbidity or any sign of growth.

## Observations

| Container | Medium | Day 3 | Day 7 | Day 14 | Growth / no growth |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test 1 | Thioglycollate | | | | |
| Test 1 | Soyabean-casein digest | | | | |
| Test 2 | Thioglycollate | | | | |
| Negative control | Both media | | | | |

## Result

The given sample showed (no growth / growth) in both media after 14 days of incubation, so it (complies / does not comply) with the test for sterility.

## Precautions

1. Work only in a laminar air flow unit or isolator with full aseptic technique; the commonest cause of a positive result in a student laboratory is contamination during the test.
2. Rinse the membrane thoroughly when the product contains an antibiotic or a preservative.
3. Handle positive controls separately and after the test samples.
4. Do not shake the tubes during incubation, as this disturbs the anaerobic layer in thioglycollate medium.
5. Record observations without opening the containers.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is 0.45 µm used instead of 0.22 µm here?** The membrane only has to retain organisms for culture, and the larger pore size filters viscous products more easily; 0.22 µm is the size used when a filter is relied on to sterilise a product.
2. **Why two different media and temperatures?** Thioglycollate at 30–35 °C recovers anaerobes and aerobic bacteria, while soyabean-casein digest at 20–25 °C recovers fungi and yeasts as well as aerobes.
3. **What is the growth promotion test?** A check that the medium can support small numbers of specified organisms, proving a negative result is meaningful.
4. **What is done if growth appears?** The result is investigated; the test may be repeated only if the growth can be shown to have come from the testing itself rather than the product.
5. **Why can a sterility test never prove a whole batch is sterile?** Only a small sample is tested and the test is destructive; sterility assurance comes from validation of the process.

# Bacteriological analysis of water

**Aim:** To test a given water sample for bacteriological quality by the multiple tube (most probable number) method and the membrane filtration method, and to perform the methylene blue reduction test.

> Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where details differ. Collect the sample in a sterile bottle and test it as soon as possible.

## Principle

Water is tested not for every organism but for **indicator organisms** of faecal pollution, chiefly **coliforms** and *Escherichia coli*, which are easy to detect and outlive most pathogens. In the **multiple tube method**, measured volumes of the sample are added to tubes of lactose broth with an inverted Durham tube; acid and gas within 48 hours is a presumptive positive, and the pattern of positive tubes is read against a **most probable number (MPN)** table to give the likely number of coliforms per 100 ml. In the **membrane filtration method**, a known volume is filtered through a **0.45 µm** membrane that retains the bacteria; the membrane is placed on a selective medium and the typical colonies are counted directly. The **methylene blue reduction test** judges the general bacterial load by how fast the dye is decolourised by bacterial metabolism.

## Requirements

Water sample in a sterile bottle, MacConkey or lactose broth (single and double strength) with Durham tubes, brilliant green bile broth, membrane filtration assembly with 0.45 µm membranes, selective agar for coliforms, sterile pipettes, methylene blue solution, incubators at 37 °C and 44 °C, colony counter.

## Procedure

**A. Multiple tube (MPN) method — presumptive coliform count**

1. Set up tubes: 1 tube with 50 ml of double-strength broth, 5 tubes with 10 ml of double-strength broth, and 5 tubes with 5 ml of single-strength broth, each with an inverted Durham tube and no air bubble.
2. Add 50 ml of sample to the large tube, 10 ml to each of the five 10 ml tubes, and 1 ml to each of the five remaining tubes.
3. Incubate at 37 °C for 24 hours; if there is no acid and gas, incubate up to 48 hours.
4. Record every tube showing **acid (colour change) and gas (a bubble in the Durham tube)** as presumptive positive.
5. Read the combination of positives against the MPN table to obtain the **presumptive coliform count per 100 ml**.

**B. Confirmed and completed tests**

6. Sub-culture each positive tube into brilliant green bile broth and incubate at 37 °C; gas confirms coliforms.
7. Incubate a parallel set at **44 °C**; gas and a positive indole test at this temperature indicate **faecal coliforms (*E. coli*)**.

**C. Membrane filtration method**

8. Filter 100 ml of the sample through a sterile 0.45 µm membrane under suction.
9. Place the membrane, grid side up, on a pad soaked in selective medium or on selective agar.
10. Incubate at 37 °C for 18–24 hours and count the typical coliform colonies. Report as colony-forming units per 100 ml.

**D. Methylene blue reduction test**

11. To 10 ml of sample add 1 ml of methylene blue solution, mix, cover and incubate at 37 °C.
12. Note the time taken for the blue colour to disappear. A short time means a heavy bacterial load.

## Observations and calculation

| Tubes with acid and gas | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 50 ml tube (1) | 10 ml tubes (out of 5) | 1 ml tubes (out of 5) |
| | | |

MPN from the table = ______ coliforms per 100 ml.

| Test | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Confirmed test at 37 °C | |
| Faecal coliform test at 44 °C | |
| Membrane filtration count | ______ CFU per 100 ml |
| Methylene blue reduction time | ______ hours |

Drinking water should contain **no coliforms in 100 ml**; the presence of *E. coli* indicates recent faecal pollution and makes the water unfit to drink.

## Result

The given water sample contained ______ coliforms per 100 ml and is therefore (fit / unfit) for drinking.

## Precautions

1. Collect the sample aseptically in a sterile bottle; if the supply is chlorinated, add sodium thiosulphate to the bottle to neutralise residual chlorine.
2. Test within a few hours, or store at about 4 °C.
3. Fill Durham tubes completely, with no air bubble before incubation.
4. Flame the mouth of bottles and tubes at every transfer.
5. Include an uninoculated tube of each medium as a sterility control.

## Viva questions

1. **Why are coliforms used as indicator organisms?** They are always present in faeces, are easy to detect, survive longer in water than most pathogens, and do not usually multiply in clean water.
2. **What is the MPN?** A statistical estimate of the number of organisms per 100 ml, obtained from the pattern of positive and negative tubes, not a direct count.
3. **Why is a parallel set incubated at 44 °C?** Growth with gas and indole production at that temperature distinguishes faecal *E. coli* from other coliforms of soil or plant origin.
4. **What pore size is used for the membrane and why?** 0.45 µm, which retains bacteria while allowing a reasonable filtration rate.
5. **What does rapid decolourisation of methylene blue mean?** A heavy bacterial load, because active metabolism quickly lowers the oxidation-reduction potential and reduces the dye to its colourless form.
practicals.title: Bacteriological analysis of water

# Evaluation of a disinfectant (phenol coefficient)

**Aim:** To determine the phenol coefficient of a given disinfectant by the Rideal-Walker method.

> Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where details differ. Phenol is corrosive; wear gloves and avoid skin contact.

## Principle

The **phenol coefficient** compares the killing power of a disinfectant with that of phenol under fixed conditions. Dilutions of phenol and of the test disinfectant are each mixed with a standard culture of *Salmonella typhi*, and sub-cultures are taken after 2.5, 5, 7.5 and 10 minutes. The coefficient is the ratio of the highest dilution of the disinfectant that kills in 7.5 minutes but not in 5 minutes, to the dilution of phenol doing the same. A value greater than 1 means the agent is more active than phenol at those dilutions.

## Requirements

Test disinfectant, phenol (as the standard), 24-hour broth culture of *Salmonella typhi* (a safe demonstration organism is substituted in teaching laboratories), sterile nutrient broth tubes, sterile pipettes, standard loop, water bath at 20 °C (or the stated temperature), stopwatch, incubator at 37 °C.

## Procedure

1. Prepare a series of dilutions of phenol, for example 1:90, 1:100, 1:110 and 1:120, and a series of dilutions of the test disinfectant over a suitable range.
2. Place 5 ml of each dilution in a test tube and leave the tubes in the water bath until all are at the same temperature.
3. At zero time add **0.5 ml of the standard culture** to the first tube, mix, and start the stopwatch. Add the culture to the remaining tubes at measured intervals so that each can be sub-cultured exactly on time.
4. At **2.5, 5, 7.5 and 10 minutes**, transfer one loopful from each tube into a separate tube of sterile nutrient broth.
5. Incubate all sub-culture tubes at 37 °C for 48 hours.
6. Record growth (+) or no growth (−) in each tube.
7. Find, for phenol and for the test disinfectant, the highest dilution that gives **no growth at 7.5 and 10 minutes but growth at 5 minutes**.

## Observations and calculation

| Dilution | 2.5 min | 5 min | 7.5 min | 10 min |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Phenol 1:90 | | | | |
| Phenol 1:100 | | | | |
| Phenol 1:110 | | | | |
| Disinfectant 1:200 | | | | |
| Disinfectant 1:250 | | | | |
| Disinfectant 1:300 | | | | |

(+ = growth, − = no growth)

Phenol coefficient = highest dilution of disinfectant killing in 7.5 but not 5 minutes ÷ highest dilution of phenol killing in 7.5 but not 5 minutes

*Worked example:* if the disinfectant satisfies the condition at 1:300 and phenol at 1:100, then the phenol coefficient = 300 ÷ 100 = **3**, so the disinfectant is about three times as active as phenol under these conditions.

## Result

The phenol coefficient of the given disinfectant was found to be ______ by the Rideal-Walker method.

## Precautions

1. Keep the temperature constant throughout; activity changes sharply with temperature.
2. Use a culture of standard age and density, since a heavier load needs longer contact.
3. Time the sub-cultures exactly with a stopwatch; use a fresh sterile loop each time.
4. Transfer the same volume at each sub-culture.
5. Include a control tube of culture with no disinfectant, which must show growth.

## Viva questions

1. **Which organism is used and why?** *Salmonella typhi*, chosen as a standard test organism of known and reproducible sensitivity.
2. **What is the main limitation of the Rideal-Walker test?** No organic matter is present, only one organism and one temperature are used, and the method suits phenol-like agents rather than all classes of disinfectant.
3. **How does the Chick-Martin test differ?** Dried yeast or faecal suspension is added to imitate organic matter, so the value obtained is lower and closer to practical use.
4. **What does a phenol coefficient of less than 1 mean?** The disinfectant is weaker than phenol at the dilutions tested.
5. **Name two other ways of evaluating a disinfectant.** The capacity (Kelsey-Sykes) test and the in-use test, along with determination of the minimum inhibitory concentration.
